# Engineering health data<br>for *secondary use*

:::: {.hero-sub}
The European Health Data Space (EHDS) establishes the legal basis for the secondary use of electronic health data across Europe. But turning electronic health data into something usable requires more than a regulation. It requires engineering.

:::: {.section-label}
The challenge
::::

## Legal permission ≠ usable data

:::: {.section-intro}
The EHDS Regulation (EU) 2025/327 [@ehds2025_327] obliges data holders across the EU to make electronic health data available for secondary use, and create the infrastructure for that data to be requested and used across borders. The Regulation entered into force on 26 March 2025, and its obligations will become applicable from 26 March 2029. The window for data holders to get EHDS ready is now. But a legal right to access data is not the same as ready-to-use data.
::::

:::::: {.split}
::::: {.split-panel}
:::: {.split-header}
The reality today
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✕
:::
Clinical data were collected to support care delivery and were not designed for reuse in research.
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✕
:::
Different healthcare providers use their own data structures, local codes, and terminology, making direct comparison impossible.
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✕
:::
Often, there is no clearly defined owner for the data's quality or lifecycle, and it ends up ageing in place, undocumented and unstable.
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✕
:::
Governance is bolted on defensively when sharing is requested, not designed in from the start.
::::
:::::

::::: {.split-panel}
:::: {.split-header}
What secondary use actually needs
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✓
:::
Data curated for specific research purposes, with clearly defined variables and agreed-upon meaning.
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✓
:::
A shared structure and vocabulary so data from different sources can be compared and combined.
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✓
:::
Clear ownership, version control, and a reliable interface that researchers can use to build pipelines.
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✓
:::
Quality and governance are embedded in the data itself, not added as an afterthought.
::::
:::::
::::::

:::: {.insight}
The EHDS explicitly recognises secondary use as a core goal, aiming to enable health data to flow across organisational and national borders to support research, public health, policymaking, and innovation. The Regulation defines *what* must be made available and discoverable, who may access which data categories, for which purposes, and under which conditions, and it even mandates dataset descriptions and a data quality and utility label. What it does not specify is *how* the data engineering is required to convert raw datasets into health data that meets those descriptions and labels.
::::

:::: {.insight}
The **GET REHDY Technical Work Package** targets precisely this gap between data collection and real‑world usefulness. What secondary use actually needs is data that behave like data products: discoverable, interoperable, and trustworthy assets that are purposefully designed for reuse in research, public health, and policymaking. By defining such health data products, together with the organisational and technical capabilities needed to govern, operate, and evolve them, **GET REHDY Technical Work Package delivers the practical foundations** that the EHDS legal framework requires but does not prescribe.
::::

:::::::
::::::::

:::::::: {.gr-section .section-alt  #paradigm}
::::::: {.section-inner}
:::: {.section-label}
The paradigm shift
::::

## From data as a by-product to Data as a Product

:::: {.section-intro}
The central concept in this work package is to treat health data not as something collected as a side effect of care, but as a product intentionally designed, owned, and maintained.
::::

:::::: {.card-grid}
::::: {.card .card-navy}
:::: {.card-number}
01 / Curation
::::
### Designed for a purpose
Instead of collecting raw records in isolated silos, a data product is curated around specific user needs and use cases, defined before any code is written.
:::::

::::: {.card .card-teal}
:::: {.card-number}
02 / Governance
::::
### Quality baked in
Governance, quality rules, semantics, and access terms are part of the design, not added when someone asks to share it. This is the posture the EHDS data quality and utility label is designed to reward.
:::::

::::: {.card .card-orange}
:::: {.card-number}
03 / Lifecycle
::::
### Clear ownership
Every data product has clear ownership: a data product owner and a domain team accountable for its quality, evolution, and maintenance throughout its lifetime.
:::::

::::: {.card .card-blue}
:::: {.card-number}
04 / Interface
::::
### A stable data contract
Consumers have a versioned interface on which they can build. Internal systems can change freely, while the published interface evolves only through explicit, versioned releases.
:::::

::::: {.card .card-blue}
:::: {.card-number}
05 / Metadata
::::
### Catalogued & discoverable
A HealthDCAT-AP record, a dataset description conforming to the draft DCAT-AP extension for health data that underpins EHDS dataset descriptions [@healthdcatap2026], is prepared for publication in EHDS catalogues, giving consumers a stable, trustworthy description.
:::::

::::::

:::: {.insight}
A well-designed data product makes data findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable [@wilkinson2016fair], and, in practice, trustworthy (FAIR-T). It is designed to reduce the compliance burden by embedding good data management and governance into the data itself, rather than bolting them on when data is shared.
::::

:::::::
::::::::

## The Data Product Canvas

:::: {.section-intro}
A data product is not discovered in the data; it is intentionally designed. The Data Product Canvas [@datameshcanvas] is a structured tool that defines all essential decisions on a single page, before a single line of code is written. It ensures that users, domain experts, and engineers share a common vision.
::::

The canvas below shows the completed blueprint for the use case example.

## Data Product design

:::: {.section-intro}
With the canvas complete, the blueprint becomes a working design document.
::::

:::::: {.flow}
::::: {.flow-step}
:::: {.flow-num}
01
::::
:::: {.flow-name}
Write
::::
:::: {.flow-desc}
Author the data contract defining the output interface
::::
:::::

::::: {.flow-step}
:::: {.flow-num}
02
::::
:::: {.flow-name}
Build
::::
:::: {.flow-desc}
The transformation pipeline is built against the data contract.
::::
:::::

::::: {.flow-step}
:::: {.flow-num}
03
::::
:::: {.flow-name}
Enforce
::::
:::: {.flow-desc}
At build time, the pipeline checks output against data contract definitions
::::
:::::

::::: {.flow-step}
:::: {.flow-num}
04
::::
:::: {.flow-name}
Test
::::
:::: {.flow-desc}
Quality rules from the data contract are applied to the materialised data
::::
:::::
::::::

:::: {.section-intro}
The central artefact in the design is the data contract, which serves as the design specification against which the transformation pipeline is built and tested. A data contract is an agreement between a data producer and its consumers [@jones2023datacontracts]. It specifies exactly what the data product exposes, its structure, semantics, quality rules, and service-level commitments, and is machine-readable, so it can be automatically enforced rather than just documented and forgotten.
::::

:::::: {.split .mb-lg}

::::: {.split-panel}
:::: {.split-header}
Without a data contract
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✕
:::
An upstream change silently breaks a downstream research pipeline, and nobody is notified until the data user spots wrong numbers.
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✕
:::
Quality is checked manually, if at all, based on implicit and undocumented expectations.
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✕
:::
Discovering what a dataset contains means asking around; metadata lives in someone's head or an outdated wiki page.
::::
:::::

::::: {.split-panel}
:::: {.split-header}
With a data contract
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✓
:::
Schema drift is detected automatically and blocks the change in the pipeline before it ever reaches a consumer.
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✓
:::
Quality rules and service-level agreements are automatically validated on every run, and they pass or fail unambiguously.
::::

:::: {.split-row}
::: {.split-icon}
✓
:::
Rich, machine-readable metadata fuels self-service discovery for both human and automated tools.
::::
:::::

::::::

## OMOP CDM & SwitchBox

:::: {.section-intro}
A well-designed local data product is a necessary foundation, but it does not always enable cross-border research. For that, we need a shared data model so a researcher's analytical code runs identically everywhere.
::::

:::::: {.pillars}
::::: {.pillar}
:::: {.pillar-icon}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 3L3 8v8l9 5 9-5V8L12 3z"/><path d="M3 8l9 5 9-5"/><path d="M12 13v8"/></svg>
```
::::
### Harmonisation
OMOP CDM brings disparate sources (EHRs, claims, registries) into a single person-centric structure using shared concepts [@ohdsi_cdm_spec]. Results from different data holders can be pooled and compared.
:::::

::::: {.pillar}
:::: {.pillar-icon}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 3v18M3 12h18"/><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="9"/></svg>
```
::::
### Statistical power
Comparable data enables evidence generation across massive, combined cross-border populations, multiplying the research value of data that would otherwise remain siloed.
:::::

::::: {.pillar}
:::: {.pillar-icon}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" aria-hidden="true"><path d="M12 22s8-4 8-10V5l-8-3-8 3v7c0 6 8 10 8 10z"/></svg>
```
::::
### Data stays local
Standardised analyses are shipped to the data, not the other way around. Patient-level records never need to be centralised; the query travels, not the data. This federated approach is proven at the European Scale by the EHDEN network [@ehden].
:::::
::::::

:::: {.section-label .mt-lg}
The SwitchBox
::::

:::: {.p-muted}
The SwitchBox [@parciak2026] is a pilot ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) tool that automates the conversion of the data product's contracted output core dataset into the OMOP CDM format. It is the bridge between the local data product and cross-border research infrastructure.
::::

Putting it together

## The end-to-end workflow

:::::: {.card-grid .grid-2}
::::: {.card .card-navy .is-linked}
:::: {.card-number}
01 / Design
::::
### [Data Product Canvas](data-product-canvas.html)
Data Product Canvas establishes purpose, ownership, consumers, and governance before engineering begins; it aligns all stakeholders on a shared blueprint.
:::::

::::: {.card .card-teal .is-linked}
:::: {.card-number}
02 / Build
::::
### Data product design
The Data Product Canvas implements the data product blueprint. The Data Product Design step delivered a data product with a contracted, versioned output port.
:::::

::::: {.card .card-orange .is-linked}
:::: {.card-number}
03 / Scale
::::
### SwitchBox & OMOP CDM
The SwitchBox ETL converts the data from the local data product into OMOP CDM format. The EHDS does not prescribe a common data model for secondary use; OMOP CDM is the model GET REHDY has chosen to close that syntactic and semantic gap [@rijnbeek2026], in line with large-scale European initiatives such as EHDEN [@ehden] and the DARWIN EU network, which already standardise on OMOP.
:::::

::::: {.card .card-purple}
:::: {.card-number}
04 / Publish
::::
### Findable
A HealthDCAT-AP [@healthdcatap2026] description of the dataset is prepared for publication in national and EU-level catalogues, enabling researchers to discover it and evaluate its suitability for their needs.
:::::
